````math
|     |                                                          |     |
|-----|----------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       b(x^{n})=\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}\hat{b}(S)\Pi_{S}(x^{n})\,,
       ```                                                       |     |

where $`\Pi_{S}(x^{n})=\Pi_{i\in S}x_{i}`$ are the orthonormal basis for
the Fourier transform and $`\{\hat{b}(S)\}_{S\subseteq[n]}`$ are the
Fourier coefficient defined by

|     |                                                |     |
|-----|------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \hat{b}(S)=\mathbb{E}b(X^{n})\Pi_{S}(X^{n})\,.
       ```                                             |     |

For $`S=\emptyset`$, we define $`\Pi_{S}(x^{n})=1`$.

Let $`\mu=\mathbb{E}[b]=\hat{b}(\emptyset)`$ be the bias, and
$`z_{i}=\hat{b}(\{i\})`$ be the level-1 Fourier coefficients. The
objective function is:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle L(b)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}I(b;Y_{i})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(H(b)-H(b|Y_{i})).`$ |  | (33) |

Since the range of $`b`$ is $`\{-1,+1\}`$, the entropy $`H(b)`$ is
determined by the bias
$`\Pr[b=1]=\frac{1+\mathbb{E}[b]}{2}=\frac{1+\mu}{2}`$, hence we can
write $`H(b)=H(\frac{1+\mu}{2})`$. Using relation (34)
from \[[25](#bib.bib25)\], we have

|     |                                                         |     |
|-----|---------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \Pr[b=1|Y_{i}=y_{i}]=\frac{1+\mu+\rho y_{i}z_{i}}{2}\,,
       ```                                                      |     |

and since the marginal distribution of $`Y_{i}`$ is uniform on
$`\{-1,+1\}`$, we get

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle H(b|Y_{i})=\frac{1}{2}\left[H(\Pr[b=1|Y_{i}=1])+H(\Pr[b=1|Y_{i}=-1])\,.\right]`$ |  | (34) |

Therefore we obtain $`H(b|Y_{i})=h_{\mu}(z_{i}),`$ where

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
h_{\mu}(z):=\frac{1}{2}H\left(\frac{1+\mu+\rho z}{2}\right)+\frac{1}{2}H\left(\frac{1+\mu-\rho z}{2}\right).
``` |  |

Let $`g_{\mu}(z)=H(b)-h_{\mu}(z)`$.
By ([33](#S8.E33 "Equation 33 ‣ Proof. ‣ Proof of Theorem ‣ 8.1.1 Part I: Generalization to Unbalanced Functions ‣ 8.1 Information Theory: The Courtade-Kumar Conjecture ‣ 8 Resolving Conjectures and Complex Derivations ‣ Accelerating Scientific Research with Gemini:Case Studies and Common Techniques")),
we want to maximize $`\sum_{i=1}^{n}g_{\mu}(z_{i})`$ subject to the
constraints on the Fourier coefficients of a Boolean function.

Step 1: Reduction to Monotone Functions. Let
$`f:\{-1,1\}^{n}\to\{-1,1\}`$ be a Boolean function. The 1-d compression
operator along coordinate $`i`$, denoted as $`\mathcal{C}_{i}`$,
rearranges the values of the function along the $`i`$-th dimension to
make it “monotone” while preserving the total number of 1s.
Specifically, for any input $`x\in\{-1,1\}^{n}`$, let
$`x=(x_{\sim i},x_{i})`$, where $`x_{\sim i}`$ are all bits except
$`i`$. The operator acts on the pair of values
$`(f(x_{\sim i},-1),f(x_{\sim i},1))`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{C}_{i}f(x_{\sim i},x_{i})=\begin{cases}1&\text{if }x_{i}=1\text{ and }f(x_{\sim i},-1)+f(x_{\sim i},1)\geq 0\\
1&\text{if }x_{i}=-1\text{ and }f(x_{\sim i},-1)+f(x_{\sim i},1)=2\\
-1&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}
``` |  | (35) |

We show that 1-d compression increases the objective function $`L(b)`$.

###### Lemma 8.3.

Let $`\tilde{b}`$ be the compression of $`b`$ along coordinate $`j`$,
making it non-decreasing in $`x_{j}`$. The Fourier coefficients satisfy:

1.  1.
    $`z_{i}(\tilde{b})=z_{i}(b)`$ for $`i\neq j`$.
2.  2.
    $`|z_{j}(\tilde{b})|\geq|z_{j}(b)|`$.

Note that $`h_{\mu}(z)=h_{\mu}(-z)`$ and the function $`h_{\mu}(z)`$ is
decreasing in $`|z|`$, hence by
Lemma [8.3](#S8.Thmtheorem3 "Lemma 8.3. ‣ Proof. ‣ Proof of Theorem ‣ 8.1.1 Part I: Generalization to Unbalanced Functions ‣ 8.1 Information Theory: The Courtade-Kumar Conjecture ‣ 8 Resolving Conjectures and Complex Derivations ‣ Accelerating Scientific Research with Gemini:Case Studies and Common Techniques")
$`h_{\mu}(z_{j}(\tilde{b}))\leq h_{\mu}(z_{j}(b))`$.

Thus, $`\sum_{i}H(b|Y_{i})`$ decreases under compression and
$`L(b)=\sum_{i}I(b;Y_{i})`$ increases. This implies that the maximum
must be attained by a function $`b`$ that is monotone along each
coordinate. We assume $`b`$ is non-decreasing, so $`z_{i}(b)\geq 0`$,
for $`i\in[n]`$, by the next lemma.

###### Lemma 8.4.

Suppose that $`b`$ is a non-decreasing Boolean function, i.e., for any
input $`x`$, changing the $`i`$-th bit from $`-1`$ to $`1`$ either
increases the function value or keeps it the same:
$`b(x_{\sim i},-1)\leq b(x_{\sim i},+1)`$. Then
$`z_{i}(b):=\hat{b}(\{i\})\geq 0`$.

We will also use the following lemma in the next step.

###### Lemma 8.5.

For any Boolean function $`b:\{-1,1\}^{n}\to\{-1,1\}`$, with
$`\mu=\mathbb{E}[b]`$ and $`z_{i}=\hat{b}(\{i\})`$ the level-1 Fourier
coefficients, we have $`z_{i}\leq 1-|\mu|`$.

Step 2: Optimization over Monotone Functions. We analyze the structure
of the optimization problem. Let $`w_{i}=z_{i}^{2}`$. Define
$`\psi_{\mu}(w)=g_{\mu}(\sqrt{w})`$. It can be shown that
$`\psi_{\mu}(w)`$ is strictly convex for $`w>0`$ (Equivalently,
$`h_{\mu}(\sqrt{w})`$ is strictly concave in $`w`$).

We want to maximize the convex function
$`\sum_{i=1}^{n}\psi_{\mu}(w_{i})`$ subject to constraints on the
Fourier coefficients.

The constraints are:

1.  1.
    $`w_{i}\geq 0`$
2.  2.
    $`\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{i}\leq 1-\mu^{2}=R^{2}`$ (Parseval’s theorem).
3.  3.
    $`w_{i}\leq(1-|\mu|)^{2}=C^{2}`$ (Since $`0\leq z_{i}\leq 1-|\mu|`$
    by
    Lemmas [8.4](#S8.Thmtheorem4 "Lemma 8.4. ‣ Proof. ‣ Proof of Theorem ‣ 8.1.1 Part I: Generalization to Unbalanced Functions ‣ 8.1 Information Theory: The Courtade-Kumar Conjecture ‣ 8 Resolving Conjectures and Complex Derivations ‣ Accelerating Scientific Research with Gemini:Case Studies and Common Techniques")
    and
    [8.5](#S8.Thmtheorem5 "Lemma 8.5. ‣ Proof. ‣ Proof of Theorem ‣ 8.1.1 Part I: Generalization to Unbalanced Functions ‣ 8.1 Information Theory: The Courtade-Kumar Conjecture ‣ 8 Resolving Conjectures and Complex Derivations ‣ Accelerating Scientific Research with Gemini:Case Studies and Common Techniques")).

The maximum of a convex function over this polytope is attained at an
extreme point. Let
$`K=R^{2}/C^{2}=(1-\mu^{2})/(1-|\mu|)^{2}=(1+|\mu|)/(1-|\mu|)`$. We
analyze two cases based on the relationship between $`n`$ and $`K`$.
Without loss of generality, assume $`\mu\geq 0`$.

Step 3: Bounding the Maximum (Case 1: $`n\geq K`$). If $`n\geq K,`$ the
constraint $`\sum w_{i}\leq R^{2}`$ is the dominant constraint. The
extreme points (up to permutation) have $`k=\lfloor K\rfloor`$
coordinates equal to $`C^{2}`$, one coordinate equal to $`\theta C^{2}`$
(where $`\theta=K-k)`$, and the rest are $`0`$. The maximum value is:

|     |                                                     |     |
|-----|-----------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       M(\mu)=k\psi_{\mu}(C^{2})+\psi_{\mu}(\theta C^{2}).
       ```                                                  |     |

We verify that $`\psi_{\mu}(0)=0.`$ Note that
$`\psi_{\mu}(0)=g_{\mu}(0)=H(b)-h_{\mu}(0)`$. Since
$`h_{\mu}(0)=H(\frac{1+\mu}{2})=H(b)`$, we have $`\psi_{\mu}(0)=0`$.
Using the convexity of $`\psi_{\mu}(w)`$ and $`\psi_{\mu}(0)=0`$:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\psi_{\mu}(\theta C^{2})=\psi_{\mu}(\theta C^{2}+(1-\theta)0)\leq\theta\psi_{\mu}(C^{2})+(1-\theta)\psi_{\mu}(0)=\theta\psi_{\mu}(C^{2}).
``` |  |

Thus, the maximum is bounded by:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
M(\mu)\leq k\psi_{\mu}(C^{2})+\theta\psi_{\mu}(C^{2})=(k+\theta)\psi_{\mu}(C^{2})=K\psi_{\mu}(C^{2})=Kg_{\mu}(C).
``` |  |

Recall that $`C=1-\mu`$ and $`K=(1+\mu)/(1-\mu)`$, and so $`\mu`$ and
$`C`$ are determined by $`K`$ as follows:

|     |                                                |     |
|-----|------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \mu=\frac{K-1}{K+1}\,,\quad C=\frac{2}{K+1}\,.
       ```                                             |     |

Let $`M_{K}(\rho):=Kg_{\mu}(C),`$ where we made the dependence on
$`\rho=1-2\alpha`$ explicit in the notation. We aim to show
$`M_{K}(\rho)\leq 1-H(\alpha)`$.

Writing $`M_{K}(\rho)`$ more explicitly, we have

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle M_{K}(\rho)`$ | $`\displaystyle=KH(b)-\frac{K}{2}H\left(\frac{1+\mu+\rho C}{2}\right)-\frac{K}{2}H\left(\frac{1+\mu-\rho C}{2}\right)`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=KH\left(\frac{K}{K+1}\right)-\frac{K}{2}H\left(\frac{K+\rho}{K+1}\right)-\frac{K}{2}H\left(\frac{K-\rho}{K+1}\right)\,,`$ |  |

where we used that $`H(b)=H(\frac{1+\mu}{2})=H(\frac{K}{K+1})`$. Note
that $`M_{1}(\rho)=1-H(\frac{1+\rho}{2})=1-H(\alpha).`$ We want to show
$`M_{K}(\rho)\leq M_{1}(\rho)`$ for $`K\geq 1`$.

Observe that $`M_{K}(0)=0`$ for all $`K`$, so it suffices to show that
the derivative with respect to $`\rho`$ satisfies
$`M_{K}^{\prime}(\rho)\leq M_{1}^{\prime}(\rho)`$.

The derivative is calculated as:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
M_{K}^{\prime}(\rho)=\frac{K}{2(K+1)\ln 2}\ln\left(\frac{(1+\rho)(K+\rho)}{(1-\rho)(K-\rho)}\right).
``` |  |

Let $`A=\frac{1+\rho}{1-\rho}`$. Then
$`M_{1}^{\prime}(\rho)=\frac{1}{2\ln 2}\ln(A)`$. The inequality
$`M_{K}^{\prime}(\rho)\leq M_{1}^{\prime}(\rho)`$ is equivalent to:

|     |                                                               |     |
|-----|---------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \frac{K}{K+1}\ln\left(A\frac{K+\rho}{K-\rho}\right)\leq\ln A.
       ```                                                            |     |

Rearranging this inequality yields:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
K\ln\left(\frac{K+\rho}{K-\rho}\right)\leq\ln A\Leftrightarrow K\ln\left(\frac{1+\rho/K}{1-\rho/K}\right)\leq\ln\left(\frac{1+\rho}{1-\rho}\right).
``` |  |

Let $`f(x)=\frac{1}{x}\ln(\frac{1+x}{1-x})`$. The inequality is
equivalent to $`f(\rho/K)\leq f(\rho)`$. The Taylor series is
$`f(x)=2\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^{2j}}{2j+1}`$, which is strictly
increasing for $`x>0`$. Since $`K\geq 1`$, we have $`\rho/K\leq\rho`$,
thus $`f(\rho/K)\leq f(\rho)`$.

The inequality $`M_{K}^{\prime}(\rho)\leq M_{1}^{\prime}(\rho)`$ holds.
Integrating from $`\rho=0`$ yields
$`M_{K}(\rho)\leq M_{1}(\rho)=1-H(\alpha)`$.

Step 4: Bounding the Maximum (Case 2: $`n<K`$). If $`n<K`$, then
$`nC^{2}<R^{2}`$. The Parseval constraint $`\sum w_{i}\leq R^{2}`$ is
inactive. We maximize the convex function $`\sum\psi_{\mu}(w_{i})`$
subject to the box constraints $`0\leq w_{i}\leq C^{2}`$. Therefore the
maximum is attained at an extreme point. In addition,
$`\psi_{\mu}(C^{2})=g_{\mu}(C)\geq 0`$ (as it represents mutual
information). Also, $`\psi_{\mu}(0)=0`$, and so
$`\psi_{\mu}(C^{2})\geq\psi_{\mu}(0)`$. Therefore, the maximum is
attained when $`w_{i}=C^{2}`$ for all $`i\in[n]`$.

The objective value is:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\psi_{\mu}(w_{i})=n\psi_{\mu}(C^{2})=ng_{\mu}(C)<Kg_{\mu}(C)=M_{K}(\rho),
``` |  |

Since $`g_{\mu}(C)\geq 0`$ (as it represents mutual information) and
$`n<K`$. From Step 3, we established $`M_{K}(\rho)\leq 1-H(\alpha)`$.

In both cases, the total mutual information is bounded by
$`1-H(\alpha)`$. ∎

##### Proof of Lemma [8.3](#S8.Thmtheorem3 "Lemma 8.3. ‣ Proof. ‣ Proof of Theorem ‣ 8.1.1 Part I: Generalization to Unbalanced Functions ‣ 8.1 Information Theory: The Courtade-Kumar Conjecture ‣ 8 Resolving Conjectures and Complex Derivations ‣ Accelerating Scientific Research with Gemini:Case Studies and Common Techniques")

We first prove that $`x_{i}(\tilde{b})=x_{i}(b)`$ for $`i\neq j`$.

Recall the definition of the Fourier coefficient
$`z_{i}(b)=\mathbb{E}[b(X^{n})X_{i}]`$. Since $`i\neq j`$, $`X_{i}`$ is
independent of $`X_{j}`$. Let $`X_{\sim j}`$ denote the bits of
$`X^{n}`$ excluding index $`j`$. We write

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
z_{i}(b)=\mathbb{E}_{X_{\sim j}}\left[\frac{X_{i}}{2}\left(b(X_{\sim j},-1)+b(X_{\sim j},1)\right)\right]
``` |  |

Now consider the compressed function $`\tilde{b}`$. By definition,
compression locally rearranges the pair
$`(b(x_{\sim j},-1),b(x_{\sim j},1))`$ into
$`(\tilde{b}(x_{\sim j},-1),\tilde{b}(x_{\sim j},1))`$ such that the sum
is preserved :

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
b(x_{\sim j},-1)+b(x_{\sim j},1)=\tilde{b}(x_{\sim j},-1)+\tilde{b}(x_{\sim j},1)
``` |  |

Substituting this back into the expectation:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle z_{i}(b)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{X_{\sim j}}\left[\frac{X_{i}}{2}\left(\tilde{b}(X_{\sim j},-1)+\tilde{b}(X_{\sim j},1)\right)\right]`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\tilde{b}(X^{n})X_{i}]=z_{i}(\tilde{b})`$ |  |

Thus, $`z_{i}(\tilde{b})=z_{i}(b)`$ for $`i\neq j`$.

We next show that $`|z_{j}(\tilde{b})|\geq|z_{j}(b)|`$. Expand the
Fourier coefficient for index $`j`$ by conditioning on $`X_{\sim j}`$:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
z_{j}(b)=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{X_{\sim j}}\left[b(X_{\sim j},1)-b(X_{\sim j},-1)\right]
``` |  |

By definition, compression locally rearranges the pair
$`(b(x_{\sim j},-1),b(x_{\sim j},1))`$ into
$`(\tilde{b}(x_{\sim j},-1),\tilde{b}(x_{\sim j},1))`$. Therefore,
$`|b(x_{\sim j},1)-b(x_{\sim j},-1)|=\tilde{b}(x_{\sim j},1)-\tilde{b}(x_{\sim j},-1)`$
for any value of $`x_{\sim j}`$. Hence,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle|z_{j}(b)|`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\left|\mathbb{E}_{X_{\sim j}}\left[b(X_{\sim j},1)-b(X_{\sim j},-1)\right]\right|`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{X_{\sim j}}\left[|b(X_{\sim j},1)-b(X_{\sim j},-1)|\right]`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{X_{\sim j}}\left[|\tilde{b}(X_{\sim j},1)-\tilde{b}(X_{\sim j},-1)|\right]`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{X_{\sim j}}\left[\tilde{b}(X_{\sim j},1)-\tilde{b}(X_{\sim j},-1)\right]=z_{j}(\tilde{b})\,,`$ |  |

where in the first step we used the convexity of absolute value
($`|\mathbb{E}[Y]|\leq\mathbb{E}[|Y|]`$). In the third equality, we used
the assumption that $`\tilde{b}`$ is non-decreasing in the $`j`$-th bit.
Note that this also implies that $`z_{j}(\tilde{b})\geq 0`$, which
completes the proof.

##### Proof of Lemma [8.4](#S8.Thmtheorem4 "Lemma 8.4. ‣ Proof. ‣ Proof of Theorem ‣ 8.1.1 Part I: Generalization to Unbalanced Functions ‣ 8.1 Information Theory: The Courtade-Kumar Conjecture ‣ 8 Resolving Conjectures and Complex Derivations ‣ Accelerating Scientific Research with Gemini:Case Studies and Common Techniques")

We can expand the expectation by conditioning on the value of the random
variable $`X_{i}`$. Since $`X`$ is uniform, $`X_{i}`$ takes values
$`-1`$ and $`+1`$ with probability $`1/2`$ each.

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle z_{i}(b)=\mathbb{E}[b(X^{n})X_{i}]=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}[b(X^{n})X_{i}\mid X_{i}=-1]+\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}[b(X^{n})X_{i}\mid X_{i}=1]`$ |  | (36) |

Substitute the value of $`X_{i}`$ into the expression:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle z_{i}(b)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}[b(X_{\sim i},-1)\cdot(-1)]+\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}[b(X_{\sim i},1)\cdot(1)]`$ |  | (37) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{x_{\sim i}}\left[b(x_{\sim i},1)-b(x_{\sim i},-1)\right]`$ |  |  |

We are given that $`b`$ is non-decreasing bit-wise. Therefore, for every
possible setting of the other bits $`x_{\sim i}`$, we have
$`b(x_{\sim i},1)\geq b(x_{\sim i},-1)`$. Thus, $`z_{i}(b)\geq 0`$.

##### Proof of Lemma [8.5](#S8.Thmtheorem5 "Lemma 8.5. ‣ Proof. ‣ Proof of Theorem ‣ 8.1.1 Part I: Generalization to Unbalanced Functions ‣ 8.1 Information Theory: The Courtade-Kumar Conjecture ‣ 8 Resolving Conjectures and Complex Derivations ‣ Accelerating Scientific Research with Gemini:Case Studies and Common Techniques")

Let $`E_{+}=\mathbb{E}[b(X)\mid X_{i}=+1]`$ and
$`E_{-}=\mathbb{E}[b(X^{n})\mid X_{i}=-1]`$ respectively denote the
average value of the function when the $`i`$-th bit is fixed to $`+1`$
and $`-1`$. Since $`b`$ outputs values in $`\{-1,1\}`$, we have
$`-1\leq E_{+},E_{-}\leq 1`$. In addition, we have

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mu`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}E_{+}+\frac{1}{2}E_{-}`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle z_{i}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[b(X)X_{i}]=\frac{1}{2}E_{+}\cdot 1+\frac{1}{2}E_{-}\cdot(-1)=\frac{E_{+}-E_{-}}{2}`$ |  |

Hence $`\mu+z_{i}=E_{+}`$ and $`\mu-z_{i}=E_{-}`$ and the claim follows
from the fact that $`E_{+}\leq 1`$ and $`E_{-}\geq-1`$.

##### Proof of Theorem [8.2](#S8.Thmtheorem2 "Theorem 8.2 (Extended Range for the Conjecture). ‣ Strengthening the High-Noise Regime Results ‣ 8.1.1 Part I: Generalization to Unbalanced Functions ‣ 8.1 Information Theory: The Courtade-Kumar Conjecture ‣ 8 Resolving Conjectures and Complex Derivations ‣ Accelerating Scientific Research with Gemini:Case Studies and Common Techniques")

##### Preliminaries and Notation

We analyze functions on the Boolean hypercube $`\{-1,1\}^{n}`$. We
follow the setup used in \[[84](#bib.bib84)\]. Let
$`f:\{-1,1\}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}`$ be a bounded, non-negative function,
normalized such that $`\mathbb{E}[f]=1`$. We assume
$`\|f\|_{\infty}\leq M`$. (When analyzing a Boolean function $`b`$, we
typically look at the indicator function of the event $`b(x)=1`$).

Let $`\alpha\in[0,1/2]`$ be the noise parameter. The noise operator
$`T_{\alpha}`$ acts on $`f`$ as
$`(T_{\alpha}f)(x)=\mathbb{E}_{y}[f(y)]`$, where $`y`$ is obtained from
$`x`$ by flipping coordinates with probability $`\alpha`$. Let
$`\rho=1-2\alpha`$. In the Fourier domain, $`T_{\alpha}`$ acts as a
multiplier:

|     |                                                |     |
|-----|------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \widehat{T_{\alpha}f}(S)=\rho^{|S|}\hat{f}(S).
       ```                                             |     |

We define the noise parameter $`\lambda=\rho^{2}=(1-2\alpha)^{2}`$. We
consider the high noise regime, where $`\lambda`$ is small.

We decompose $`f`$ into its even part $`f_{0}`$ and odd part $`f1`$:

|     |                                                                    |     |
|-----|--------------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       f_{0}(x)=\frac{f(x)+f(-x)}{2},\quad f_{1}(x)=\frac{f(x)-f(-x)}{2}.
       ```                                                                 |     |

Note that $`\mathbb{E}[f_{0}]=1`$.

We define the noisy versions:

|     |                                            |     |
|-----|--------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       F=T_{\alpha}f_{0},\quad Z=T_{\alpha}f_{1}.
       ```                                         |     |

Note that $`T_{\alpha}f=F+Z`$. We define $`Y=F-1`$. Since
$`\mathbb{E}[F]=1`$, we have $`\mathbb{E}[Y]=0`$.

The Fourier coefficients satisfy
$`\hat{F}(S)=\lambda^{|S|/2}\hat{f_{0}}(S)`$ and
$`\hat{Z}(S)=\lambda^{|S|/2}\hat{f_{1}}(S)`$. $`F`$ (and $`Y`$) are
supported on even Fourier levels, while $`Z`$ is supported on odd
levels.

The level 1 Fourier weight is $`L_{1}(f)=L_{1}(f_{1})`$.

We utilize the entropy decomposition established in \[[84](#bib.bib84)\]
(Lemma 6.2):

###### Lemma 8.6 (Entropy Decomposition).

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{Ent}(T_{\alpha}f)\leq\mathrm{Ent}(F)+\frac{1}{2\ln 2}\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{Z^{2}}{F}\right]+O\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{Z^{4}}{F^{3}}\right]\right).
``` |  |

It is known that $`\mathrm{Ent}(F)=O(\lambda^{2})`$ (Lemma 5.4 in
\[[84](#bib.bib84)\]).

We also rely on a crucial dominance property.

###### Lemma 8.7 (Dominance).

$`F\geq 0`$ and $`|Z|\leq F`$.

###### Proof.

Note that by definition of the even and odd parts of $`f`$, we have

|     |                                     |                          |     |
|-----|-------------------------------------|--------------------------|-----|
|     | $`\displaystyle f_{0}(x)+f_{1}(x)`$ | $`\displaystyle=2f(x)`$  |     |
|     | $`\displaystyle f_{0}(x)-f_{1}(x)`$ | $`\displaystyle=2f(-x)`$ |     |

Since $`f\geq 0`$, we have $`|f_{1}(x)|\leq f_{0}(x)`$. The noise
operator $`T_{\alpha}`$ is a positive operator, preserving
non-negativity and dominance. Thus
$`|Z|=|T_{\alpha}f_{1}|\leq T_{\alpha}|f_{1}|\leq T_{\alpha}f_{0}=F`$. ∎

##### Hypercontractivity and Moment Bounds

We rely on the Bonami-Beckner Hypercontractivity Theorem. A standard
application is for homogeneous polynomials.

###### Corollary 8.8 (Hypercontractivity for Homogeneous Polynomials).

Let $`h_{k}`$ be a homogeneous polynomial of degree $`k`$. For
$`q\geq 2`$,

|     |                                                 |     |
|-----|-------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \|h_{k}\|_{q}\leq(\sqrt{q-1})^{k}\|h_{k}\|_{2}.
       ```                                              |     |

We must be careful when applying this to functions supported on multiple
levels. We use the Minkowski inequality combined with Corollary
[8.8](#S8.Thmtheorem8 "Corollary 8.8 (Hypercontractivity for Homogeneous Polynomials). ‣ Hypercontractivity and Moment Bounds ‣ 8.1.1 Part I: Generalization to Unbalanced Functions ‣ 8.1 Information Theory: The Courtade-Kumar Conjecture ‣ 8 Resolving Conjectures and Complex Derivations ‣ Accelerating Scientific Research with Gemini:Case Studies and Common Techniques")
to establish rigorous moment bounds.

###### Lemma 8.9 (Moment Bounds).

Assuming $`f`$ is bounded by $`M`$, the following bounds hold as
$`\lambda\to 0`$:

1.  1.
    $`\mathbb{E}[Y^{2}]=O(\lambda^{2})`$.
2.  2.
    $`\mathbb{E}[|Y|^{3}]=O(\lambda^{3})`$.
3.  3.
    $`\mathbb{E}[Z^{2}]=\lambda L_{1}(f)+O(\lambda^{3})`$.
4.  4.
    $`\mathbb{E}[Z^{4}]=O(\lambda^{2})`$.
5.  5.
    $`\mathbb{E}[Z^{2}Y]=O(\lambda^{2})`$.

###### Proof.

We assume $`\lambda`$ is small enough (e.g., $`3\lambda<1`$). Since
$`f`$ is bounded, its $`L_{2}`$ norm is also bounded
($`\|f\|_{2}\leq M`$).

Part 1: $`\mathbb{E}[Y^{2}]=O(\lambda^{2})`$. $`Y`$ is supported on even
levels $`\geq 2`$.

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[Y^{2}]`$ | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{k\geq 2,\text{even}}\lambda^{k}\sum_{|S|=k}\hat{f_{0}}(S)^{2}`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\leq\lambda^{2}\sum_{S\neq\emptyset}\hat{f_{0}}(S)^{2}=\lambda^{2}\text{Var}(f_{0})=O(\lambda^{2}).`$ |  |

Part 2: $`\mathbb{E}[|Y|^{3}]=O(\lambda^{3})`$. We analyze
$`Y=Y_{2}+Y_{\geq 4}`$ using the $`L_{3}`$ norm.

1.  1.
    Bounding $`\|Y_{2}\|_{3}`$. Use $`q=3,k=2`$. The constant is 2.

    |     |                                   |     |
    |-----|-----------------------------------|-----|
    |     |
           ``` math
           \|Y_{2}\|_{3}\leq 2\|Y_{2}\|_{2}.
           ```                                |     |

    $`\|Y_{2}\|_{2}^{2}=O(\lambda^{2})`$. Thus,
    $`\|Y_{2}\|_{3}=O(\lambda)`$.
2.  2.
    Bounding $`\|Y_{\geq 4}\|_{3}`$.

    |  |  |  |
    |----|----|----|
    |  |
    ``` math
    \|Y_{\geq 4}\|3\leq\sum{k\geq 4,\text{even}}\|Y_{k}\|3\leq\sum{k\geq 4,\text{even}}M(\sqrt{2\lambda})^{k}=O(\lambda^{2}).
    ``` |  |
3.  3.
    Combining the bounds. $`\|Y\|_{3}=O(\lambda)`$. Therefore,
    $`\mathbb{E}[|Y|^{3}]=O(\lambda^{3})`$.

Part 3: $`\mathbb{E}[Z^{2}]=\lambda L_{1}(f)+O(\lambda^{3})`$. $`Z`$ is
supported on odd levels $`\geq 1`$.

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[Z^{2}]`$ | $`\displaystyle=\lambda L_{1}(f_{1})+\sum_{k\geq 3,\text{odd}}\lambda^{k}\sum_{|S|=k}\hat{f_{1}}(S)^{2}`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\lambda L_{1}(f)+O(\lambda^{3}).`$ |  |

Part 4: $`\mathbb{E}[Z^{4}]=O(\lambda^{2})`$. We decompose
$`Z=Z_{1}+Z_{\geq 3}`$. We use the Minkowski inequality for the
$`L_{4}`$ norm: $`\|Z\|4\leq\|Z_{1}\|_{4}+\|Z{\geq 3}\|_{4}`$.

1.  1.
    Bounding $`\|Z_{1}\|_{4}`$. $`Z_{1}`$ is degree 1. Use Corollary
    [8.8](#S8.Thmtheorem8 "Corollary 8.8 (Hypercontractivity for Homogeneous Polynomials). ‣ Hypercontractivity and Moment Bounds ‣ 8.1.1 Part I: Generalization to Unbalanced Functions ‣ 8.1 Information Theory: The Courtade-Kumar Conjecture ‣ 8 Resolving Conjectures and Complex Derivations ‣ Accelerating Scientific Research with Gemini:Case Studies and Common Techniques")
    ($`q=4,k=1`$).

    |     |                                         |     |
    |-----|-----------------------------------------|-----|
    |     |
           ``` math
           \|Z_{1}\|_{4}\leq\sqrt{3}\|Z_{1}\|_{2}.
           ```                                      |     |

    $`\|Z_{1}\|_{2}^{2}=O(\lambda)`$. Thus,
    $`\|Z_{1}\|_{4}=O(\lambda^{1/2})`$.
2.  2.
    Bounding $`\|Z_{\geq 3}\|_{4}`$. Use Minkowski inequality on
    $`Z_{\geq 3}=\sum_{k\geq 3,\text{odd}}Z_{k}`$.

    |     |                                                           |     |
    |-----|-----------------------------------------------------------|-----|
    |     |
           ``` math
           \|Z_{\geq 3}\|4\leq\sum{k\geq 3,\text{odd}}\|Z_{k}\|_{4}.
           ```                                                        |     |

    Applying hypercontractivity to each $`Z_{k}`$:

    |     |                                               |     |
    |-----|-----------------------------------------------|-----|
    |     |
           ``` math
           \|Z_{k}\|_{4}\leq(\sqrt{3})^{k}\|Z_{k}\|_{2}.
           ```                                            |     |

    Since $`\|\hat{f}_{k}\|_{2}\leq M`$,
    $`\|Z_{k}\|_{2}\leq M\lambda^{k/2}`$.

    |     |                                           |     |
    |-----|-------------------------------------------|-----|
    |     |
           ``` math
           \|Z_{k}\|_{4}\leq M(\sqrt{3\lambda})^{k}.
           ```                                        |     |

    We sum this geometric series:

    |  |  |  |
    |----|----|----|
    |  |
    ``` math
    \|Z_{\geq 3}\|4\leq M\sum{k\geq 3,\text{odd}}(\sqrt{3\lambda})^{k}=M\frac{(\sqrt{3\lambda})^{3}}{1-3\lambda}=O(\lambda^{3/2}).
    ``` |  |
3.  3.
    Combining the bounds.

    |     |                                                                   |     |
    |-----|-------------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
    |     |
           ``` math
           \|Z\|_{4}\leq O(\lambda^{1/2})+O(\lambda^{3/2})=O(\lambda^{1/2}).
           ```                                                                |     |

    Therefore, $`\mathbb{E}[Z^{4}]=\|Z\|_{4}^{4}=O(\lambda^{2})`$.

Part 5: $`\mathbb{E}[Z^{2}Y]=O(\lambda^{2})`$. We use the Cauchy-Schwarz
inequality:

|     |                                                                    |     |
|-----|--------------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       |\mathbb{E}[Z^{2}Y]|\leq\sqrt{\mathbb{E}[Z^{4}]\mathbb{E}[Y^{2}]}.
       ```                                                                 |     |

Using Part 4 and Part 1:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
|\mathbb{E}[Z^{2}Y]|\leq\sqrt{O(\lambda^{2})\cdot O(\lambda^{2})}=O(\lambda^{2}).
``` |  |

∎

##### Higher Order Term

We now bound the higher order term in the entropy decomposition (Lemma
[8.6](#S8.Thmtheorem6 "Lemma 8.6 (Entropy Decomposition). ‣ Preliminaries and Notation ‣ 8.1.1 Part I: Generalization to Unbalanced Functions ‣ 8.1 Information Theory: The Courtade-Kumar Conjecture ‣ 8 Resolving Conjectures and Complex Derivations ‣ Accelerating Scientific Research with Gemini:Case Studies and Common Techniques")).

###### Lemma 8.10 (Higher Order Term).

$`\mathbb{E}[Z^{4}/F^{3}]=O(\lambda^{2})`$.

###### Proof.

We use a constant threshold $`\Delta=1/2`$ to split the expectation.

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{Z^{4}}{F^{3}}\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{Z^{4}}{F^{3}}\mathbb{I}{F\leq 1/2}\right]+\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{Z^{4}}{F^{3}}\mathbb{I}{F>1/2}\right].
``` |  |

Term 2 (F is large): When $`F>1/2`$, $`1/F^{3}<8`$.

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{Z^{4}}{F^{3}}\mathbb{I}_{F>1/2}\right]\leq 8\mathbb{E}[Z^{4}].
``` |  |

By Lemma
[8.9](#S8.Thmtheorem9 "Lemma 8.9 (Moment Bounds). ‣ Hypercontractivity and Moment Bounds ‣ 8.1.1 Part I: Generalization to Unbalanced Functions ‣ 8.1 Information Theory: The Courtade-Kumar Conjecture ‣ 8 Resolving Conjectures and Complex Derivations ‣ Accelerating Scientific Research with Gemini:Case Studies and Common Techniques")(4),
$`\mathbb{E}[Z^{4}]=O(\lambda^{2})`$. So Term 2 is $`O(\lambda^{2})`$.

Term 1 (F is small): By Lemma
[8.7](#S8.Thmtheorem7 "Lemma 8.7 (Dominance). ‣ Preliminaries and Notation ‣ 8.1.1 Part I: Generalization to Unbalanced Functions ‣ 8.1 Information Theory: The Courtade-Kumar Conjecture ‣ 8 Resolving Conjectures and Complex Derivations ‣ Accelerating Scientific Research with Gemini:Case Studies and Common Techniques"),
$`|Z|\leq F`$. So $`Z^{4}/F^{3}\leq F`$.

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{Z^{4}}{F^{3}}\mathbb{I}{F\leq 1/2}\right]\leq\mathbb{E}[F\mathbb{I}{F\leq 1/2}].
``` |  |

Since $`F\leq 1/2`$ on this indicator,

|     |                                                                 |     |
|-----|-----------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \mathbb{E}[F\mathbb{I}_{F\leq 1/2}]\leq\frac{1}{2}P(F\leq 1/2).
       ```                                                              |     |

$`P(F\leq 1/2)=P(Y\leq-1/2)`$. By Chebyshev’s inequality and Lemma
[8.9](#S8.Thmtheorem9 "Lemma 8.9 (Moment Bounds). ‣ Hypercontractivity and Moment Bounds ‣ 8.1.1 Part I: Generalization to Unbalanced Functions ‣ 8.1 Information Theory: The Courtade-Kumar Conjecture ‣ 8 Resolving Conjectures and Complex Derivations ‣ Accelerating Scientific Research with Gemini:Case Studies and Common Techniques")(1):

|     |                                                       |     |
|-----|-------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       P(|Y|\geq 1/2)\leq 4\mathbb{E}[Y^{2}]=O(\lambda^{2}).
       ```                                                    |     |

So Term 1 is $`O(\lambda^{2})`$. ∎

##### Optimal Asymptotic Entropy Bound

We now prove the main technical result of this section, achieving the
optimal $`O(\lambda^{2})`$ error bound by employing a direct Taylor
expansion.

###### Theorem 8.11 (Optimal Asymptotic Entropy Bound).

For any bounded nonnegative non-zero function $`f`$ with
$`\mathbb{E}[f]=1`$:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{Ent}(T_{\alpha}f)\leq\left(\frac{1}{2\ln 2}L_{1}(f)\right)\cdot\lambda+O(\lambda^{2}).
``` |  |

The proof, detailed below, relies on a direct Taylor expansion approach
combined with rigorous moment bounds derived using hypercontractivity.
Crucially, we employ a careful application of the Minkowski inequality
over the Fourier decomposition to establish the necessary higher-moment
bounds. The optimality of this bound is demonstrated by the fact that
the $`O(\lambda^{2})`$ error rate is tight for Boolean dictatorship
functions.

###### Proof.

We start from the entropy decomposition (Lemma
[8.6](#S8.Thmtheorem6 "Lemma 8.6 (Entropy Decomposition). ‣ Preliminaries and Notation ‣ 8.1.1 Part I: Generalization to Unbalanced Functions ‣ 8.1 Information Theory: The Courtade-Kumar Conjecture ‣ 8 Resolving Conjectures and Complex Derivations ‣ Accelerating Scientific Research with Gemini:Case Studies and Common Techniques")):

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{Ent}(T_{\alpha}f)\leq\mathrm{Ent}(F)+\frac{1}{2\ln 2}\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{Z^{2}}{F}\right]+O\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{Z^{4}}{F^{3}}\right]\right).
``` |  |

We know $`\mathrm{Ent}(F)=O(\lambda^{2})`$ and by Lemma
[8.10](#S8.Thmtheorem10 "Lemma 8.10 (Higher Order Term). ‣ Higher Order Term ‣ 8.1.1 Part I: Generalization to Unbalanced Functions ‣ 8.1 Information Theory: The Courtade-Kumar Conjecture ‣ 8 Resolving Conjectures and Complex Derivations ‣ Accelerating Scientific Research with Gemini:Case Studies and Common Techniques"),
the error term is $`O(\lambda^{2})`$. We analyze
$`B=\mathbb{E}[Z^{2}/F]`$.

We use the Taylor expansion of $`1/F=1/(1+Y)`$ around $`Y=0`$ with the
exact remainder:

|     |                                      |     |
|-----|--------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \frac{1}{1+Y}=1-Y+\frac{Y^{2}}{1+Y}.
       ```                                   |     |

This holds when $`F=1+Y>0`$. Let $`S_{+}=\{x:F(x)>0\}`$.

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
B=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{Z^{2}}{F}\mathbb{I}{S+}\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[Z^{2}\left(1-Y+\frac{Y^{2}}{F}\right)\mathbb{I}{S+}\right].
``` |  |

Term 1 (Expansion): $`E_{T}=\mathbb{E}[Z^{2}(1-Y)\mathbb{I}{S+}]`$. By
Lemma
[8.7](#S8.Thmtheorem7 "Lemma 8.7 (Dominance). ‣ Preliminaries and Notation ‣ 8.1.1 Part I: Generalization to Unbalanced Functions ‣ 8.1 Information Theory: The Courtade-Kumar Conjecture ‣ 8 Resolving Conjectures and Complex Derivations ‣ Accelerating Scientific Research with Gemini:Case Studies and Common Techniques"),
if $`F(x)=0`$, then $`Z(x)=0`$. The indicator is redundant.

|     |                                             |     |
|-----|---------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       E_{T}=\mathbb{E}[Z^{2}]-\mathbb{E}[Z^{2}Y].
       ```                                          |     |

By Lemma
[8.9](#S8.Thmtheorem9 "Lemma 8.9 (Moment Bounds). ‣ Hypercontractivity and Moment Bounds ‣ 8.1.1 Part I: Generalization to Unbalanced Functions ‣ 8.1 Information Theory: The Courtade-Kumar Conjecture ‣ 8 Resolving Conjectures and Complex Derivations ‣ Accelerating Scientific Research with Gemini:Case Studies and Common Techniques")(3)
and (5):

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle E_{T}`$ | $`\displaystyle=(\lambda L_{1}(f)+O(\lambda^{3}))-O(\lambda^{2})=\lambda L_{1}(f)+O(\lambda^{2}).`$ |  |

Term 2 (Remainder):
$`R_{T}=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{Z^{2}Y^{2}}{F}\mathbb{I}{S+}\right]`$.
Using dominance $`|Z|\leq F`$, $`Z^{2}/F\leq F`$.

|     |                                                                  |     |
|-----|------------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       R_{T}\leq\mathbb{E}[FY^{2}\mathbb{I}{S+}]\leq\mathbb{E}[FY^{2}].
       ```                                                               |     |

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbb{E}[FY^{2}]=\mathbb{E}[(1+Y)Y^{2}]=\mathbb{E}[Y^{2}]+\mathbb{E}[Y^{3}].
``` |  |

By Lemma
[8.9](#S8.Thmtheorem9 "Lemma 8.9 (Moment Bounds). ‣ Hypercontractivity and Moment Bounds ‣ 8.1.1 Part I: Generalization to Unbalanced Functions ‣ 8.1 Information Theory: The Courtade-Kumar Conjecture ‣ 8 Resolving Conjectures and Complex Derivations ‣ Accelerating Scientific Research with Gemini:Case Studies and Common Techniques")(1)
and (2), $`R_{T}=O(\lambda^{2})+O(\lambda^{3})=O(\lambda^{2})`$.

Combining the terms for $`B`$:

|     |                                    |     |
|-----|------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       B=\lambda L_{1}(f)+O(\lambda^{2}).
       ```                                 |     |

Substituting this back into the entropy decomposition:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathrm{Ent}(T_{\alpha}f)`$ | $`\displaystyle\leq O(\lambda^{2})+\frac{1}{2\ln 2}(\lambda L_{1}(f)+O(\lambda^{2}))+O(\lambda^{2})`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\frac{L_{1}(f)}{2\ln 2}\lambda+O(\lambda^{2}).`$ |  |

We next show that the $`O(\lambda^{2})`$ error term is asymptotically
tight. We demonstrate this by analyzing the dictatorship functions which
are believed to maximize the entropy (and mutual information).

Consider the Boolean dictatorship function $`f(x)=x_{1}`$. The mutual
information is exactly the channel capacity, $`I(f(X);Y)=1-H(\alpha)`$,
where $`H(\alpha)`$ is the binary entropy function (in bits). We analyze
the Taylor expansion of the capacity around $`\alpha=1/2`$ (where
$`\rho=0`$).

Recall $`\rho=1-2\alpha`$ and $`\lambda=\rho^{2}`$. The expansion of the
binary entropy function $`H(\alpha)`$ around $`\alpha=1/2`$ yields

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
H(\alpha)=1-\frac{1}{2\ln 2}\rho^{2}-\frac{1}{12\ln 2}\rho^{4}+O(\rho^{6}).
``` |  |

Therefore, the capacity is:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
1-H(\alpha)=\frac{1}{2\ln 2}\lambda+\frac{1}{12\ln 2}\lambda^{2}+O(\lambda^{3}).
``` |  |

For the dictatorship function, $`L_{1}(f)=1`$. Thus, the expansion
matches the form in the theorem statement:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
I(f(X);Y)=\left(\frac{L_{1}(f)}{2\ln 2}\right)\lambda+\Theta(\lambda^{2}).
``` |  |

Since the expansion for the maximizing function includes a
$`\Theta(\lambda^{2})`$ term, the general upper bound established in the
theorem statement cannot be asymptotically improved beyond
$`O(\lambda^{2})`$. ∎

##### Implications and Applications

The optimal error bound established in the previous section has
significant consequences for the structural properties of highly
informative functions and the range of validity of the Courtade-Kumar
conjecture.

##### Linear Fourier Concentration

The $`O(\lambda^{2})`$ error bound allows us to derive the strongest
possible Fourier concentration result within this asymptotic framework.

###### Theorem 8.12 (Linear Fourier Concentration).

Let $`f`$ be a Boolean function satisfying $`c\leq\mathbb{E}f\leq 1/2`$
(for some absolute constant $`c>0`$). If $`I(f(X);Y)\geq 1-H(\alpha)`$,
then

|     |                                            |     |
|-----|--------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \sum_{|S|\geq 2}\hat{f}(S)^{2}=O(\lambda).
       ```                                         |     |

###### Proof.

Let $`p=\mathbb{E}f`$. We utilize the connection:
$`I(f(X);Y)=\mathrm{Ent}(T_{\alpha}f)+\mathrm{Ent}(T_{\alpha}(1-f))`$.

We apply Theorem
[8.11](#S8.Thmtheorem11 "Theorem 8.11 (Optimal Asymptotic Entropy Bound). ‣ Optimal Asymptotic Entropy Bound ‣ 8.1.1 Part I: Generalization to Unbalanced Functions ‣ 8.1 Information Theory: The Courtade-Kumar Conjecture ‣ 8 Resolving Conjectures and Complex Derivations ‣ Accelerating Scientific Research with Gemini:Case Studies and Common Techniques")
by normalizing $`f`$. Using
$`\mathrm{Ent}(h)=\mathbb{E}[h]\cdot\mathrm{Ent}(h/\mathbb{E}[h])`$, we
have $`\mathrm{Ent}(T_{\alpha}f)=p\cdot\mathrm{Ent}(T_{\alpha}(f/p))`$.
Applying the theorem to $`f/p`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathrm{Ent}(T_{\alpha}f)`$ | $`\displaystyle\leq p\left(\frac{L_{1}(f/p)}{2\ln 2}\lambda+O(\lambda^{2})\right)`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\frac{L_{1}(f)}{p(2\ln 2)}\lambda+O(\lambda^{2}).`$ |  |

The $`O(\lambda^{2})`$ constant remains controlled because $`p`$ is
bounded away from 0 by $`c`$. Applying the same logic to $`1-f`$, and
noting $`L_{1}(f)=L_{1}(1-f)`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle I(f(X);Y)`$ | $`\displaystyle\leq\left(\frac{1}{p}+\frac{1}{1-p}\right)\frac{L_{1}(f)}{2\ln 2}\lambda+O(\lambda^{2})`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\frac{1}{p(1-p)}\frac{L_{1}(f)}{2\ln 2}\lambda+O(\lambda^{2}).`$ |  |

We use the Taylor expansion of the channel capacity:
$`1-H(\alpha)=\frac{\lambda}{2\ln 2}-O(\lambda^{2})`$. Combining this
with the assumption $`I(f(X);Y)\geq 1-H(\alpha)`$:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\frac{\lambda}{2\ln 2}+O(\lambda^{2})\leq\frac{1}{p(1-p)}\frac{L_{1}(f)}{2\ln 2}\lambda+O(\lambda^{2}).
``` |  |

Dividing by $`\lambda/(2\ln 2)`$:

|     |                                                     |     |
|-----|-----------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       1+O(\lambda)\leq\frac{L_{1}(f)}{p(1-p)}+O(\lambda).
       ```                                                  |     |

Rearranging:

|     |                                 |     |
|-----|---------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       p(1-p)-O(\lambda)\leq L_{1}(f).
       ```                              |     |

By Parseval’s identity, $`\sum_{S\neq\emptyset}\hat{f}(S)^{2}=p(1-p)`$.
Therefore, the Fourier weight on levels 2 and higher is:

|     |                                                                |     |
|-----|----------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \sum_{|S|\geq 2}\hat{f}(S)^{2}=p(1-p)-L_{1}(f)\leq O(\lambda).
       ```                                                             |     |

∎

This linear concentration is a significant improvement over the
$`O(\lambda^{1/3})`$ bound established in \[[84](#bib.bib84)\].

##### Extended Range for the Conjecture

The improved Fourier concentration directly translates to proving the
Courtade-Kumar conjecture for a wider range of the noise parameter
$`\lambda`$.

We are now ready to prove
Theorem [8.2](#S8.Thmtheorem2 "Theorem 8.2 (Extended Range for the Conjecture). ‣ Strengthening the High-Noise Regime Results ‣ 8.1.1 Part I: Generalization to Unbalanced Functions ‣ 8.1 Information Theory: The Courtade-Kumar Conjecture ‣ 8 Resolving Conjectures and Complex Derivations ‣ Accelerating Scientific Research with Gemini:Case Studies and Common Techniques").
We recall the theorem below.

###### Theorem 8.13 (Main Result - Extended Range).

There exists an absolute constant $`\delta_{opt}>0`$ such that if the
noise parameter $`\lambda\leq\delta_{opt}`$, the Courtade-Kumar
conjecture holds. Furthermore, $`\delta_{opt}`$ is strictly larger than
the threshold established using the $`O(\lambda^{4/3})`$ error bound in
\[[84](#bib.bib84)\].

###### Proof.

The proof strategy follows the established path in \[[84](#bib.bib84)\],
relying on the combination of Fourier concentration and structural
theorems for Boolean functions.

Theorem
[8.12](#S8.Thmtheorem12 "Theorem 8.12 (Linear Fourier Concentration). ‣ Linear Fourier Concentration ‣ 8.1.1 Part I: Generalization to Unbalanced Functions ‣ 8.1 Information Theory: The Courtade-Kumar Conjecture ‣ 8 Resolving Conjectures and Complex Derivations ‣ Accelerating Scientific Research with Gemini:Case Studies and Common Techniques")
implies that a highly informative function $`f`$ has most of its Fourier
mass on level 1. Define $`\xi:=\sum_{|S|\geq 2}\hat{f}(S)^{2}`$. Theorem
5.5 in \[[84](#bib.bib84)\] at high level states that such a function
must be close to a dictatorship. Concretely, by this theorem we have

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle|\mathbb{E}[f]|`$ | $`\displaystyle=O(\xi\sqrt{\ln(1/\xi)}),`$ |  | (38) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\hat{f}(\{k\})^{2}`$ | $`\displaystyle\geq 1-\xi-O(\xi^{2}\ln(1/\xi))\,`$ |  | (39) |

for some $`k\in[n]`$.⁹⁹ 9 Note that in our notation $`f`$ takes its
values in $`\{-1,1\}`$ which corresponds to the $`g`$ notation
in \[[84](#bib.bib84)\]. The next step involves analyzing the mutual
information of near-dictatorship functions (Theorem 1.14
in \[[84](#bib.bib84)\]), by which
Conjecture [29](#S8.E29 "Equation 29 ‣ The Courtade-Kumar Conjecture ‣ 8.1.1 Part I: Generalization to Unbalanced Functions ‣ 8.1 Information Theory: The Courtade-Kumar Conjecture ‣ 8 Resolving Conjectures and Complex Derivations ‣ Accelerating Scientific Research with Gemini:Case Studies and Common Techniques")
holds provided that

|     |                                                    |     |      |
|-----|----------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     | $`\displaystyle\xi\sqrt{\ln(1/\xi)}\leq c_{0}\,,`$ |     | (40) |

for a small absolute constant $`c_{0}`$.

There is also another constraint that needs to be satisfied and is
implicit in the proof of Theorem 1.14 \[[84](#bib.bib84)\], which we
discuss next. Define $`\alpha,\beta\geq 0`$ as follows:
$`\beta=-(1/2)\hat{f}(\emptyset)=-(1/2)\mathbb{E}[f]`$ and
$`\hat{f}(\{k\})=(1-\alpha)(1-2\beta)`$. Also set
$`\gamma:=\alpha+\beta`$. Then, another condition used in Proof of
 \[[84](#bib.bib84), Theorem 1.14 (page 30)\] is that

|     |                                                        |     |      |
|-----|--------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     | $`\displaystyle\lambda+\gamma\ln(1/\gamma)\leq c_{1}`$ |     | (41) |

for some small absolute constant $`c_{1}>0`$.
Invoking ([38](#S8.E38 "Equation 38 ‣ Proof. ‣ Extended Range for the Conjecture ‣ 8.1.1 Part I: Generalization to Unbalanced Functions ‣ 8.1 Information Theory: The Courtade-Kumar Conjecture ‣ 8 Resolving Conjectures and Complex Derivations ‣ Accelerating Scientific Research with Gemini:Case Studies and Common Techniques"))
and ([39](#S8.E39 "Equation 39 ‣ Proof. ‣ Extended Range for the Conjecture ‣ 8.1.1 Part I: Generalization to Unbalanced Functions ‣ 8.1 Information Theory: The Courtade-Kumar Conjecture ‣ 8 Resolving Conjectures and Complex Derivations ‣ Accelerating Scientific Research with Gemini:Case Studies and Common Techniques")),
$`\gamma=O(\xi\sqrt{\ln(1/\xi)})`$. In
Theorem [8.12](#S8.Thmtheorem12 "Theorem 8.12 (Linear Fourier Concentration). ‣ Linear Fourier Concentration ‣ 8.1.1 Part I: Generalization to Unbalanced Functions ‣ 8.1 Information Theory: The Courtade-Kumar Conjecture ‣ 8 Resolving Conjectures and Complex Derivations ‣ Accelerating Scientific Research with Gemini:Case Studies and Common Techniques"),
we proved that $`\xi=O(\lambda)`$ and so
$`\gamma=O(\lambda\sqrt{\ln(1/\lambda)})`$. Since
$`\ln(1/\gamma)=O(\ln(1/\lambda))`$, we have:

|     |                                                       |     |
|-----|-------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \gamma\ln(1/\gamma)=O(\lambda(\ln(1/\lambda))^{3/2}).
       ```                                                    |     |

Hence,
condition ([41](#S8.E41 "Equation 41 ‣ Proof. ‣ Extended Range for the Conjecture ‣ 8.1.1 Part I: Generalization to Unbalanced Functions ‣ 8.1 Information Theory: The Courtade-Kumar Conjecture ‣ 8 Resolving Conjectures and Complex Derivations ‣ Accelerating Scientific Research with Gemini:Case Studies and Common Techniques"))
becomes

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\lambda+\lambda(\ln(1/\lambda))^{3/2}\leq c^{\prime}_{1}`$ |  | (42) |

for some absolute constant $`c^{\prime}_{1}>0`$. Furthermore, using that
$`\xi=O(\lambda)`$,
condition ([40](#S8.E40 "Equation 40 ‣ Proof. ‣ Extended Range for the Conjecture ‣ 8.1.1 Part I: Generalization to Unbalanced Functions ‣ 8.1 Information Theory: The Courtade-Kumar Conjecture ‣ 8 Resolving Conjectures and Complex Derivations ‣ Accelerating Scientific Research with Gemini:Case Studies and Common Techniques"))
is equivalent to

|     |                                                            |     |      |
|-----|------------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     | $`\displaystyle\lambda\sqrt{\ln(1/\lambda)}\leq c_{0}\,.`$ |     | (43) |

Condition ([42](#S8.E42 "Equation 42 ‣ Proof. ‣ Extended Range for the Conjecture ‣ 8.1.1 Part I: Generalization to Unbalanced Functions ‣ 8.1 Information Theory: The Courtade-Kumar Conjecture ‣ 8 Resolving Conjectures and Complex Derivations ‣ Accelerating Scientific Research with Gemini:Case Studies and Common Techniques"))
already implies Condition
([43](#S8.E43 "Equation 43 ‣ Proof. ‣ Extended Range for the Conjecture ‣ 8.1.1 Part I: Generalization to Unbalanced Functions ‣ 8.1 Information Theory: The Courtade-Kumar Conjecture ‣ 8 Resolving Conjectures and Complex Derivations ‣ Accelerating Scientific Research with Gemini:Case Studies and Common Techniques")).
In summary,
Condition ([42](#S8.E42 "Equation 42 ‣ Proof. ‣ Extended Range for the Conjecture ‣ 8.1.1 Part I: Generalization to Unbalanced Functions ‣ 8.1 Information Theory: The Courtade-Kumar Conjecture ‣ 8 Resolving Conjectures and Complex Derivations ‣ Accelerating Scientific Research with Gemini:Case Studies and Common Techniques"))
defines the threshold $`\delta_{opt}`$.

In contrast, the analysis in \[[84](#bib.bib84)\], based on the
$`O(\lambda^{4/3})`$ error bound, yielded a Fourier concentration of
$`O(\lambda^{1/3})`$. This led to the bound
$`\gamma=O(\lambda^{1/3}\sqrt{\ln(1/\lambda)})`$ and a condition
dominated by $`O(\lambda^{1/3}(\ln(1/\lambda))^{3/2})`$.

Since $`1>1/3`$, the function $`x(\ln(1/x))^{3/2}`$ approaches zero
significantly faster than $`x^{1/3}(\ln(1/x))^{3/2}`$ as $`x\to 0`$.
Therefore, the threshold $`\delta_{opt}`$ satisfying the new, tighter
inequality is strictly larger than the threshold derived from the
$`O(\lambda^{4/3})`$ analysis. ∎

#### 8.1.2 Part II: The Unsymmetrized Conjecture and the Li-Médard’s Conjecture

##### Problem Context

Beyond the main conjecture, Li and Médard \[[70](#bib.bib70)\] proposed
related conjectures on the $`L_{\alpha}`$-norm of the noise-stability
operator $`T_{p}f(x)=P(f(Y)=1\mid X=x)`$. They conjectured that for
balanced functions, the “unsymmetrized” norm
$`N_{\alpha}(f)=\sum(T_{p}f(x))^{\alpha}`$ is maximized by a
dictatorship. This “Unsymmetrized Conjecture” implies the Courtade-Kumar
conjecture.

##### AI Contribution

We provided the AI system with the research paper \[[10](#bib.bib10)\]
as primary input, and prompted it to prove the Unsymmetrized Conjecture
(Conjecture 1) or the Li-Médard Conjecture (Conjecture 3) therein.

- •
  Analyzing Relaxations: The AI analyzed a relaxation of the problem to
  maximizing $`\mathcal{J}(q)=\sum q_{x}\log q_{x}`$ under moment
  constraints. It identified that the dictatorship is a saddle point
  (not a global max) for this specific relaxation, revealing why
  standard approaches fail.
- •
  Structural Insights: It proved that any maximizer of the relaxed
  problem must be a distribution supported on at most two points (Lemma
  [8.15](#S8.Thmtheorem15 "Lemma 8.15. ‣ Related Conjectures on Functionals of 𝑓. ‣ 8.1.2 Part II: The Unsymmetrized Conjecture and the Li-Médard’s Conjecture ‣ 8.1 Information Theory: The Courtade-Kumar Conjecture ‣ 8 Resolving Conjectures and Complex Derivations ‣ Accelerating Scientific Research with Gemini:Case Studies and Common Techniques")).
- •
  Local Optimality: It proved that the dictatorship function is a *local
  maximum* for the optimization problem over the Boolean Hull (Lemma
  [8.18](#S8.Thmtheorem18 "Lemma 8.18. ‣ Related Conjectures on Functionals of 𝑓. ‣ 8.1.2 Part II: The Unsymmetrized Conjecture and the Li-Médard’s Conjecture ‣ 8.1 Information Theory: The Courtade-Kumar Conjecture ‣ 8 Resolving Conjectures and Complex Derivations ‣ Accelerating Scientific Research with Gemini:Case Studies and Common Techniques")).
- •
  Monotonicity: It established that the maximizer must be a monotone
  function (Lemma
  [8.17](#S8.Thmtheorem17 "Lemma 8.17. ‣ Related Conjectures on Functionals of 𝑓. ‣ 8.1.2 Part II: The Unsymmetrized Conjecture and the Li-Médard’s Conjecture ‣ 8.1 Information Theory: The Courtade-Kumar Conjecture ‣ 8 Resolving Conjectures and Complex Derivations ‣ Accelerating Scientific Research with Gemini:Case Studies and Common Techniques")).

##### Technical Details: Unsymmetrized Courtade-Kumar Conjecture and the Li-Médard Conjecture

We begin by recalling the Courtade-Kumar conjecture
\[[25](#bib.bib25)\]. Let $`X`$ be a random variable uniformly
distributed over the $`n`$-dimensional Hamming cube $`\{0,1\}^{n}`$. We
define $`Y`$ as a noisy observation of $`X`$ obtained by passing each
coordinate of $`X`$ through a memoryless Binary Symmetric Channel (BSC)
with crossover probability $`p\in(0,1/2)`$.

Courtade and Kumar conjectured that for any Boolean function
$`f:\{0,1\}^{n}\to\{0,1\}`$, the mutual information between the function
output $`f(Y)`$ and the original input $`X`$ is bounded by:

|     |                      |     |
|-----|----------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       I(f(Y);X)\leq 1-h(p)
       ```                   |     |

where $`h(p)=-p\log_{2}p-(1-p)\log_{2}(1-p)`$ denotes the binary entropy
function.

The conjecture posits that this maximum mutual information is achieved
when $`f`$ is a dictatorship function—that is, a function that depends
solely on a single input coordinate, such as $`f(Y)=Y_{i}`$ for any
$`i\in\{1,\dots,n\}`$.

##### Related Conjectures on Functionals of $`f`$.

Beyond the primary Courtade-Kumar conjecture, several related
conjectures have been proposed in \[[70](#bib.bib70), [1](#bib.bib1)\].
These works generally posit that dictatorship functions are the
maximizers for various functionals of Boolean functions. Of particular
relevance is the work of Li and Médard \[[70](#bib.bib70)\], which
focuses on balanced Boolean functions (where $`\mathbb{E}[f]=1/2`$).

They investigate the $`L_{\alpha}`$-norm of the noise-stability
operator, defined as:

|     |                             |     |      |
|-----|-----------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       T_{p}f(x)=P(f(Y)=1\mid X=x)
       ```                          |     | (44) |

Li and Médard conjecture that among all balanced functions $`f`$, the
quantity $`N_{\alpha}(f)`$ is maximized by a dictatorship function
$`f_{0}`$ for $`1\leq\alpha\leq 2`$. Specifically, they consider the
unsymmetrized and symmetrized versions of these norms:

- •
  Unsymmetrized Norm:
  $`N_{\alpha}(f)=\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^{n}}(T_{p}f(x))^{\alpha}`$
- •
  Symmetrized Norm:
  $`N^{\text{sym}}_{\alpha}(f)=\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^{n}}\left[(T_{p}f(x))^{\alpha}+(1-T_{p}f(x))^{\alpha}\right]`$

The Entropy Connection. For a balanced function $`f`$, the mutual
information $`I(f(Y);X)`$ can be expressed in terms of the noise
operator. Since $`H(f(Y))=1`$ for balanced functions, we have:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle I(f(Y);X)`$ | $`\displaystyle=1-H(f(Y)\mid X)`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=1-\frac{1}{2^{n}}\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^{n}}h(T_{p}f(x))`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=1+\frac{1}{2^{n}}\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^{n}}\left[T_{p}f(x)\log_{2}T_{p}f(x)+(1-T_{p}f(x))\log_{2}(1-T_{p}f(x))\right]`$ |  | (45) |

This decomposition motivates an “unsymmetrized” version of the
Courtade-Kumar conjecture, which focuses solely on the term
$`\sum T_{p}f(x)\log_{2}T_{p}f(x)`$.

Comparison of Conjectures. Let $`f`$ be a balanced Boolean function and
$`f_{0}`$ be a dictatorship function. The various conjectures are
summarized in
Table [3](#S8.T3 "Table 3 ‣ Related Conjectures on Functionals of 𝑓. ‣ 8.1.2 Part II: The Unsymmetrized Conjecture and the Li-Médard’s Conjecture ‣ 8.1 Information Theory: The Courtade-Kumar Conjecture ‣ 8 Resolving Conjectures and Complex Derivations ‣ Accelerating Scientific Research with Gemini:Case Studies and Common Techniques").

| Conjecture | Name | Formal Statement |
|----|----|----|
| Conjecture 1 | Unsymmetrized C-K | $`\sum T_{p}f(x)\log T_{p}f(x)\leq\sum T_{p}f_{0}(x)\log T_{p}f_{0}(x)`$ |
| Conjecture 2 | Courtade-Kumar | $`I(f(Y);X)\leq 1-h(p)`$ |
| Conjecture 3 | Li-Médard ($`L_{\alpha}`$) | $`N_{\alpha}(f)\leq N_{\alpha}(f_{0})`$ for $`1\leq\alpha\leq 2`$ |
| Conjecture 4 | Symmetrized Li-Médard | $`N^{\text{sym}}_{\alpha}(f)\leq N^{\text{sym}}_{\alpha}(f_{0})`$ for $`1\leq\alpha\leq 2`$ |

Table 3: Summary of related conjectures for balanced Boolean functions.

Prior work in \[[10](#bib.bib10)\] has established the following logical
relationships between these conjectures:

|     |                                                              |     |      |
|-----|--------------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       \begin{matrix}\text{Conjecture 1}&\iff&\text{Conjecture 3}\\
       \Downarrow&&\Downarrow\\
       \text{Conjecture 2}&\iff&\text{Conjecture 4}\end{matrix}
       ```                                                           |     | (46) |

Specifically, if the $`L_{\alpha}`$-norm conjectures hold, the
corresponding Courtade-Kumar conjectures (symmetrized and unsymmetrized)
follow for all balanced functions.

We prompted the Gemini AI system to prove either Conjecture 1 or
Conjecture 3.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 18: Model identification of open problem and progress direction

The system specifically analyzed a relaxed version of the optimization
problem given by:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\text{Maximize }\mathcal{J}(q):=\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^{n}}q_{x}\log q_{x}`$ |  | (47) |

subject to the constraints $`\sum q_{x}=N_{1}(f_{0})`$ and
$`\sum q_{x}^{2}\leq N_{2}(f_{0})`$. The model’s analysis identified
that the dictatorship distribution constitutes a saddle point for this
relaxed problem. Consequently, this suggested that the current
relaxation is insufficient to prove the primary conjecture, as the
dictatorship function does not emerge as a definitive global maximizer
under these constraints. Following an iterative review of the system’s
detailed technical reports, we derived the following result (which we
later noted is consistent with findings in \[[10](#bib.bib10),
[20](#bib.bib20), [70](#bib.bib70)\]):

###### Lemma 8.14.

For any balanced Boolean function $`f`$, $`N_{2}(f)\leq N_{2}(f_{0})`$
and $`N^{\text{sym}}_{2}(f)\leq N^{\text{sym}}_{2}(f_{0})`$, where
equality holds if and only if $`f`$ is a dictatorship function.

Leveraging this result, we provided the system with a specific strategy
to pursue further refinements of the proof.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 19: Model identification of open problem and progress direction

It revealed a subtle logical gap in the initial argument. To address
this, the system investigated the relaxed optimization problems,
demonstrating that the optimal solution is characterized by a two-point
distribution. By leveraging this structural property, the system
provided an analytical upper bound for the maximum objective value
achievable by any balanced Boolean function.

###### Lemma 8.15.

Consider maximizing $`\mathcal{J}(q)`$ given
by ([47](#S8.E47 "Equation 47 ‣ Related Conjectures on Functionals of 𝑓. ‣ 8.1.2 Part II: The Unsymmetrized Conjecture and the Li-Médard’s Conjecture ‣ 8.1 Information Theory: The Courtade-Kumar Conjecture ‣ 8 Resolving Conjectures and Complex Derivations ‣ Accelerating Scientific Research with Gemini:Case Studies and Common Techniques"))
over the set
$`K_{1}=\{q:\mathbb{E}[q]=1/2,\text{Var}(q)\leq\rho^{2}/4\}`$. Then the
maximizing distribution is supported on two points
$`\{0,(1+\rho^{2})/2\}`$, achieving the objective value:
$`V=2^{n-1}\ln\left(\frac{1+\rho^{2}}{2}\right)`$.

Note that the $`\rho^{2}/4`$ bound on the variance comes from
Lemma [8.14](#S8.Thmtheorem14 "Lemma 8.14. ‣ Related Conjectures on Functionals of 𝑓. ‣ 8.1.2 Part II: The Unsymmetrized Conjecture and the Li-Médard’s Conjecture ‣ 8.1 Information Theory: The Courtade-Kumar Conjecture ‣ 8 Resolving Conjectures and Complex Derivations ‣ Accelerating Scientific Research with Gemini:Case Studies and Common Techniques")
as $`N_{2}(f_{0})=(1+\rho^{2})/4`$. We also asked the AI system to plot
the upper bound established by
Lemma [8.15](#S8.Thmtheorem15 "Lemma 8.15. ‣ Related Conjectures on Functionals of 𝑓. ‣ 8.1.2 Part II: The Unsymmetrized Conjecture and the Li-Médard’s Conjecture ‣ 8.1 Information Theory: The Courtade-Kumar Conjecture ‣ 8 Resolving Conjectures and Complex Derivations ‣ Accelerating Scientific Research with Gemini:Case Studies and Common Techniques")
along with the value achieved by the dictatorship functions (see
Figure [20](#S8.F20 "Figure 20 ‣ Related Conjectures on Functionals of 𝑓. ‣ 8.1.2 Part II: The Unsymmetrized Conjecture and the Li-Médard’s Conjecture ‣ 8.1 Information Theory: The Courtade-Kumar Conjecture ‣ 8 Resolving Conjectures and Complex Derivations ‣ Accelerating Scientific Research with Gemini:Case Studies and Common Techniques").)

![Refer to caption](2602.03837v3/plot.png)

Figure 20: Comparison of the objective functional values for the
two-point distribution relaxation (upper bound), given by
Lemma [8.15](#S8.Thmtheorem15 "Lemma 8.15. ‣ Related Conjectures on Functionals of 𝑓. ‣ 8.1.2 Part II: The Unsymmetrized Conjecture and the Li-Médard’s Conjecture ‣ 8.1 Information Theory: The Courtade-Kumar Conjecture ‣ 8 Resolving Conjectures and Complex Derivations ‣ Accelerating Scientific Research with Gemini:Case Studies and Common Techniques"),
and the dictatorship function as the correlation parameter $`\rho`$
varies from 0 to 1.

We next sought to tighten the relaxation by establishing an
$`L_{\infty}`$ bound for the functions $`q`$ realizable by balanced
Boolean functions. However, the system identified a technical flaw in
our proposed bound and provided a concrete counter-example, leading us
to pivot our strategy.

Our subsequent approach focused on leveraging the inverse of the noise
operator. Given a correlation parameter $`\rho`$, if $`q=T_{\rho}f`$,
the original function can be recovered via the inverse transformation
$`f=T_{1/\rho}q`$. Recall that the noise operator is linear and can be
expressed as:

|     |                                               |     |
|-----|-----------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       T_{\rho}f(x)=\sum_{y\in\{0,1\}^{n}}P(x,y)f(y)
       ```                                            |     |

where the transition kernel is determined by the Hamming distance
$`d(x,y)`$. To refine the optimization space, we relaxed the strict
Boolean constraint $`f(x)\in\{0,1\}`$ to a pointwise box constraint,
requiring $`0\leq(T_{1/\rho}q)_{x}\leq 1`$ for all $`x`$. Combining this
with the established constraints on the first and second moments of
$`q`$, we defined the following relaxed constraint set $`K`$:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
K:=\left\{q:\mathbb{E}[q]=\frac{1}{2},\quad\text{Var}(q)\leq\frac{\rho^{2}}{4},\quad 0\leq(T_{1/\rho}q)_{x}\leq 1\right\}
``` |  |

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 21: Model identification of open problem and progress direction

Interestingly it showed that the variance constraint is already implied
by the other two. In addition, it showed that this relaxation is indeed
tight, as discussed next.

Let $`\mathcal{F}_{B}`$ be the set of balanced Boolean functions
$`f:\{0,1\}^{n}\to\{0,1\}`$ and define the entropy functional
$`\Phi(f)=\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^{n}}h((T_{\rho}f)(x))`$ with
$`h(t)=t\ln t`$. Let $`\mathcal{G}`$ be the Boolean Hull (functions
$`g:\{0,1\}^{n}\to[0,1]`$ with $`\mathbb{E}[g]=1/2`$). Let
$`K=T_{\rho}(\mathcal{G})`$ be the feasible set for $`q`$, which can
then be characterized by the mean constraint $`\mathbb{E}[q]=1/2`$ and
the pointwise box constraints $`0\leq T_{1/\rho}q\leq 1`$.

###### Lemma 8.16.

(Convex Relaxation and Tightness). Maximizing $`\Phi(f)`$ over
$`\mathcal{F}_{B}`$ is equivalent to maximizing $`\mathcal{J}(q)`$ over
$`K`$.

This equivalence is an important milestone as it transforms the initial
optimization over discrete Boolean functions into a continuous convex
optimization.

In addition, it proves two other structural properties of the solution.

###### Lemma 8.17.

(Monotonicity). If $`f\in\mathcal{F}_{B}`$ maximizes $`\Phi(f)`$, then
$`f`$ can be assumed to be monotone.

###### Lemma 8.18.

(Local optimality). A dictatorship function is a local maximum of the
problem of maximizing $`\mathcal{J}(q)`$ over $`K`$.

The AI system also attempted to prove global optimality of the
dictatorship functions by an inductive proof and identifies the
remaining gaps. Concretely, consider the restrictions of the function
$`f`$ to the $`(n-1)`$-dimensional sub-cubes. Let
$`f_{0},f_{1}:\{0,1\}^{n-1}\to\{0,1\}`$ be defined by
$`f_{0}(x^{\prime})=f(x^{\prime},0)`$ and
$`f_{1}(x^{\prime})=f(x^{\prime},1)`$. Furthermore, let
$`T^{\prime}_{\rho}`$ denote the noise operator acting on $`n-1`$
variables, and let $`g_{i}=T^{\prime}_{\rho}f_{i}`$ represent the
noise-evolved versions of these sub-functions. The functional
$`\Phi(f)`$ admits the following decomposition:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Phi(f)=\sum_{x^{\prime}\in\{0,1\}^{n-1}}J(g_{0}(x^{\prime}),g_{1}(x^{\prime}))
``` |  |

where the kernel $`J(a,b)`$ is defined as
$`J(a,b)=h(pa+\varepsilon b)+h(\varepsilon a+pb)`$, with
$`h(t)=t\ln(t)`$, and the parameters $`p`$ and $`\varepsilon`$ are given
by $`p=\frac{1+\rho}{2}`$ and $`\varepsilon=\frac{1-\rho}{2}`$.

The system then continues with the following response given the above
notation.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

We next conducted several further iterations of prompting to explore the
inductive path. Specifically, we attempted to solidify the connection
with Mrs. Gerber’s Lemma—which was also previously used in
\[[84](#bib.bib84)\] to prove C-K conjecture in the high-noise regime.
However, while the system could identify the relevance of the lemma, it
ultimately failed to complete the formal analytical steps required for
the proof.

Observations on AI-Assisted Research. Our interactions with the system
on these theoretical problems yielded several key insights into its
utility as a research partner:

- •
  Confirmation Bias in Prompting: The system exhibits a tendency to
  support the position or hypothesis presented in the prompt. When
  tasked with proving open-ended conjectures that are not necessarily
  true, it often attempts to bridge logical gaps with “hand-wavy”
  arguments that do not withstand rigorous scrutiny. We found that
  performance improves significantly when using neutral prompts (e.g.,
  “prove or refute”), which encourages the system to evaluate multiple
  directions in parallel.
- •
  Effectiveness in Refutation: The system is remarkably adept at
  identifying counterexamples and pinpointing the “crux” of a problem.
  When provided with a precise but flawed idea, it can often explain
  exactly why a particular strategy fails, making it a valuable tool for
  early-stage proof debugging.

##### Proof of Lemma [8.15](#S8.Thmtheorem15 "Lemma 8.15. ‣ Related Conjectures on Functionals of 𝑓. ‣ 8.1.2 Part II: The Unsymmetrized Conjecture and the Li-Médard’s Conjecture ‣ 8.1 Information Theory: The Courtade-Kumar Conjecture ‣ 8 Resolving Conjectures and Complex Derivations ‣ Accelerating Scientific Research with Gemini:Case Studies and Common Techniques")

To formally prove that the optimal distribution $`q_{x}`$ is supported
on at most two points, we analyze the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT)
conditions. This structural approach reveals how the moment constraints
necessitate a sparse distribution. We seek to maximize
$`f(q)=\sum_{x}q_{x}\ln q_{x}`$, which is equivalent to minimizing
$`-\sum_{x}q_{x}\ln q_{x}`$. Defining $`M=2^{n}`$ as the size of the
Hamming cube, we construct the Lagrangian $`\mathcal{L}`$ with
multipliers $`\lambda`$ and $`\mu`$ for the mean and variance
constraints:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}(q,\lambda,\mu)=-\sum_{x=1}^{M}q_{x}\ln q_{x}+\lambda\left(\sum_{x}q_{x}-\frac{M}{2}\right)+\mu\left(\sum_{x}q_{x}^{2}-C\right)
``` |  |

where the quadratic constraint $`C=\frac{M(1+\rho^{2})}{4}`$ assumes the
variance constraint $`\text{Var}(q)\leq\rho^{2}/4`$ is active at the
maximum. Setting the partial derivative with respect to each $`q_{x}`$
to zero gives:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial q_{x}}=-(\ln q_{x}+1)+\lambda+2\mu q_{x}=0
``` |  |

Rearranging this yields the transcendental equation
$`\ln q_{x}-2\mu q_{x}=\lambda-1`$. Let $`g(q)=\ln q-2\mu q`$. Any
optimal value of $`q_{x}`$ must lie at the intersection of $`g(q)`$ and
the constant $`\lambda-1`$. Since $`g^{\prime\prime}(q)=-1/q^{2}`$,
which is strictly negative for all $`q>0`$, $`g(q)`$ is strictly
concave. A strictly concave function can intersect a horizontal line at
most at two distinct points, proving that the optimal $`q_{x}`$ can take
at most two values, $`a`$ and $`b`$. Let $`k`$ be the multiplicity of
the value $`a`$, such that $`M-k`$ indices take the value $`b`$. The
linear and quadratic constraints provide the following system:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle ka+(M-k)b`$ | $`\displaystyle=M/2,`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle ka^{2}+(M-k)b^{2}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{M(1+\rho^{2})}{4}.`$ |  |

Solving for $`a(k)`$ and $`b(k)`$ in terms of $`k`$, we find:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
a(k)=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{\rho}{2}\sqrt{\frac{M-k}{k}},\quad b(k)=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\rho}{2}\sqrt{\frac{k}{M-k}}.
``` |  |

The objective function can then be expressed as
$`F(k)=k\phi(a(k))+(M-k)\phi(b(k))`$, where $`\phi(t)=t\ln t`$. To
determine the behavior of $`F(k)`$, we examine its derivative
$`F^{\prime}(k)`$ via implicit differentiation of the constraints:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
F^{\prime}(k)=(\phi(a)-\phi(b))-(a-b)\frac{\phi^{\prime}(a)+\phi^{\prime}(b)}{2}
``` |  |

Assuming $`a>b`$, we utilize the integral representation
$`\phi(a)-\phi(b)=\int_{b}^{a}\phi^{\prime}(t)dt`$ to rewrite the
derivative:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
F^{\prime}(k)=\int_{b}^{a}\phi^{\prime}(t)dt-(a-b)\frac{\phi^{\prime}(a)+\phi^{\prime}(b)}{2}
``` |  |

This expression represents the difference between the integral of
$`\phi^{\prime}(t)`$ and the trapezoidal area under the chord connecting
$`(b,\phi^{\prime}(b))`$ and $`(a,\phi^{\prime}(a))`$. Calculating the
derivatives of $`\phi(t)=t\ln t`$, we find $`\phi^{\prime}(t)=\ln t+1`$,
$`\phi^{\prime\prime}(t)=1/t`$, and
$`\phi^{\prime\prime\prime}(t)=-1/t^{2}`$. Since
$`\phi^{\prime\prime\prime}(t)<0`$ for all $`t>0`$, the function
$`\phi^{\prime}(t)`$ is strictly concave. For a strictly concave
function, the area under the curve is strictly greater than the area of
the trapezoid defined by the chord. Consequently, $`F^{\prime}(k)>0`$,
meaning the objective function $`F(k)`$ is strictly increasing over its
feasible domain. The maximum is therefore achieved at the largest
possible value of $`k`$. Given the non-negativity constraint
$`b(k)\geq 0`$, the maximum $`k`$ occurs when $`b=0`$. Solving for $`k`$
in this boundary condition yields $`k=\frac{M}{1+\rho^{2}}`$, which
results in $`a=\frac{1+\rho^{2}}{2}`$. Substituting these values back
into the objective yields the maximum value
$`V=\frac{M}{2}\ln\left(\frac{1+\rho^{2}}{2}\right)=2^{n-1}\ln\left(\frac{1+\rho^{2}}{2}\right)`$.

##### Proof of Lemma [8.16](#S8.Thmtheorem16 "Lemma 8.16. ‣ Related Conjectures on Functionals of 𝑓. ‣ 8.1.2 Part II: The Unsymmetrized Conjecture and the Li-Médard’s Conjecture ‣ 8.1 Information Theory: The Courtade-Kumar Conjecture ‣ 8 Resolving Conjectures and Complex Derivations ‣ Accelerating Scientific Research with Gemini:Case Studies and Common Techniques")

Since $`T_{\rho}`$ is linear, $`K`$ is a convex polytope. Since
$`\mathcal{J}(q)`$ is strictly convex, its maximum over $`K`$ is
attained at an extreme point. The extreme points of $`K`$ are the images
of the extreme points of $`\mathcal{G}`$, which are $`\mathcal{F}_{B}`$
(the set of balanced Boolean functions). Thus, maximizing $`\Phi(f)`$
over $`\mathcal{F}_{B}`$ is equivalent to maximizing $`\mathcal{J}(q)`$
over $`K`$.

##### Proof of Lemma [8.17](#S8.Thmtheorem17 "Lemma 8.17. ‣ Related Conjectures on Functionals of 𝑓. ‣ 8.1.2 Part II: The Unsymmetrized Conjecture and the Li-Médard’s Conjecture ‣ 8.1 Information Theory: The Courtade-Kumar Conjecture ‣ 8 Resolving Conjectures and Complex Derivations ‣ Accelerating Scientific Research with Gemini:Case Studies and Common Techniques")

We use decomposition along the $`n`$-th coordinate. Let
$`f_{0}(x^{\prime})=f(x^{\prime},0)`$ and
$`f_{1}(x^{\prime})=f(x^{\prime},1)`$. Let $`T^{\prime}_{\rho}`$ be the
noise operator on $`n-1`$ variables. Let
$`g_{i}=T^{\prime}_{\rho}f_{i}`$. The functional decomposes as:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Phi(f)=\sum_{x^{\prime}\in\{0,1\}^{n-1}}J(g_{0}(x^{\prime}),g_{1}(x^{\prime})),
``` |  |

where $`J(a,b)=h(pa+\varepsilon b)+h(\varepsilon a+pb)`$, with
$`p=(1+\rho)/2`$ and $`\varepsilon=(1-\rho)/2`$. Let $`m=(a+b)/2`$ and
$`d=(b-a)/2`$. Then $`J(a,b)=h(m-\rho d)+h(m+\rho d)`$. Since $`h`$ is
strictly convex, $`J`$ is strictly increasing in $`|d|`$ for fixed
$`m`$.

Consider the polarization $`f^{*}`$ defined by
$`f^{*}_{0}=\min(f_{0},f_{1})`$ and $`f^{*}_{1}=\max(f_{0},f_{1})`$.
Note that $`f^{*}`$ is balanced since
$`f^{*}_{0}+f^{*}_{1}=f_{0}+f_{1}`$. Let
$`g^{*}_{i}=T^{\prime}_{\rho}f^{*}_{i}`$. The means are preserved
pointwise: $`m^{*}(x^{\prime})=m(x^{\prime})`$. The differences are
$`d(x^{\prime})=T^{\prime}_{\rho}((f_{1}-f_{0})/2)`$ and
$`d^{*}(x^{\prime})=T^{\prime}_{\rho}(|f_{1}-f_{0}|/2)`$.

Since $`T^{\prime}_{\rho}`$ is a positive operator (its kernel is
non-negative as it represents probabilities), we have the inequality
$`|T^{\prime}_{\rho}(u)|\leq T^{\prime}_{\rho}(|u|)`$. Thus,
$`|d(x^{\prime})|\leq d^{*}(x^{\prime})`$. Since $`J`$ increases with
$`|d|`$, $`\Phi(f)\leq\Phi(f^{*})`$. By repeatedly applying this
polarization, we conclude that the maximum must be attained by a
monotone function.

##### Proof of Lemma [8.18](#S8.Thmtheorem18 "Lemma 8.18. ‣ Related Conjectures on Functionals of 𝑓. ‣ 8.1.2 Part II: The Unsymmetrized Conjecture and the Li-Médard’s Conjecture ‣ 8.1 Information Theory: The Courtade-Kumar Conjecture ‣ 8 Resolving Conjectures and Complex Derivations ‣ Accelerating Scientific Research with Gemini:Case Studies and Common Techniques")

We verify that the Dictatorship is a local maximum by checking the KKT
conditions for maximizing $`\mathcal{J}(q)`$ over the polytope $`K`$.
The set $`K`$ is defined by the constraints $`0\leq(Mq)_{x}\leq 1`$ and
$`\sum q_{x}=N/2`$, where $`M=T_{1/\rho}`$.

We formulate the KKT conditions for maximization subject to
$`g_{1}(q):=-Mq\leq 0`$ and $`g_{2}(q):=Mq-1\leq 0`$. The gradient
condition is $`\nabla\mathcal{J}(q)=M(\mu-\lambda)`$, where
$`\lambda,\mu\geq 0`$ are the multipliers for $`g_{1}`$ and $`g_{2}`$
respectively (ignoring the equality constraint which adds a constant
shift $`\nu\mathbf{1}`$). Let $`\gamma=\mu-\lambda`$ and $`g:=Mq`$.
Complementary slackness implies:

- •
  If $`g_{x}=0`$, then $`\mu_{x}=0`$, which implies
  $`\gamma_{x}\leq 0`$.
- •
  If $`g_{x}=1`$, then $`\lambda_{x}=0`$, which implies
  $`\gamma_{x}\geq 0`$.

Let $`q^{*}`$ be the noise operator applied to the dictatorship function
$`f_{D}(x)=x_{1}`$, i.e., $`q^{*}=T_{\rho}(f_{D})`$. Consequently,
$`g^{*}=Mq^{*}=T_{1/\rho}(q^{*})=f_{D}`$. Let $`A=\{x\mid x_{1}=1\}`$
and $`B=\{x\mid x_{1}=0\}`$. We have $`g^{*}=1`$ on $`A`$ and
$`g^{*}=0`$ on $`B`$. We therefore require $`\gamma\geq 0`$ on $`A`$ and
$`\gamma\leq 0`$ on $`B`$.

The gradient condition is given by
$`h^{\prime}(q^{*}_{y})=(M\gamma)_{y}+\nu`$. Let $`v=M\gamma`$. Since
$`q^{*}`$ takes values $`a`$ on $`B`$ and $`b`$ on $`A`$, $`v`$ must be
constant on $`A`$ and $`B`$:

|     |                              |     |      |
|-----|------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       v(x)=c_{0}+c_{1}\chi_{1}(x),
       ```                           |     | (48) |

where $`\chi_{1}(x)=(-1)^{x_{1}}`$. Calculating $`c_{1}`$, we obtain

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
c_{1}=\frac{h^{\prime}(a)-h^{\prime}(b)}{2}=\frac{1}{2}\ln(a/b)=-\operatorname{artanh}(\rho)<0,
``` |  | (49) |

where we used that $`a=\frac{1-\rho}{2}`$ and $`b=\frac{1+\rho}{2}`$, by
definition of the noise operator. We also have
$`\gamma=T_{\rho}v=c_{0}+\rho c_{1}\chi_{1}(x)`$. The resulting
constraints on $`\gamma`$ are:

- •
  On $`A`$ ($`\chi_{1}=-1`$):
  $`c_{0}-\rho c_{1}\geq 0\implies c_{0}\geq\rho c_{1}`$.
- •
  On $`B`$ ($`\chi_{1}=1`$):
  $`c_{0}+\rho c_{1}\leq 0\implies c_{0}\leq-\rho c_{1}`$.

We require $`\rho c_{1}\leq c_{0}\leq-\rho c_{1}`$. Given that
$`c_{1}<0`$ and $`\rho>0`$, we have $`\rho c_{1}<0<-\rho c_{1}`$. This
interval is non-empty (e.g., $`c_{0}=0`$ is a valid solution). Thus, the
Dictatorship satisfies the KKT conditions and is a local maximum.

### 8.2 NP-hardness: Ratio Difference Maximization (RDM)

Written by Ravi Kumar and Silvio Lattanzi (on behalf of coauthors).

#### Problem Context

In a recent work \[[22](#bib.bib22)\], together with Flavio
Chierichetti, Mirko Giacchini, Alessandro Panconesi, Erasmo Tani, and
Andrew Tomkins, we were studying Multinomial Logits (MNLs), also known
as Plackett–Luce models, that describe user preferences by assigning a
weight to each item in a universe. When a user is presented a subset of
items, they select one with probability proportional to its weight. In
the paper, we consider the problem of learning an MNL by sampling from
the conditional distributions induced on subsets of the universe.

Interestingly, even computing the worst-case error on arbitrary size
subsets of the universe turns out to be a non-trivial problem.
In \[[22](#bib.bib22)\] we introduce several approximation algorithms
for this tasks. We also had the intuition that the problem was related
to SUBSET-SUM and most likely NP-hard but we felt that the reduction was
not immediate and hence we decided to test Gemini with such a question.
We were happily surprised by receiving a zero-shot correct proof within
a few minutes.

We then asked also to prove NP-hardness for a variation of the
problem.

AI Contribution

Given only the formal definition of the Ratio Difference Maximization
(RDM) problem, the AI zero-shot generated a flawless, polynomial-time
NP-hardness reduction from the SUBSET-SUM problem. Upon a subsequent
prompt, it successfully proved the NP-hardness of a related variation
(MAX-DIFF-RATIO) using a similarly rigorous reduction.

More specifically, we used a math rigor prompt and we asked the model to
show that the *Ratio Difference Maximization (RDM)* problem is NP-hard.
This is the prompt that we used:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

This is the output provided by Gemini that we verified to be correct:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Given the success of the first attempt, using the same prompt structure,
we also asked to show that a variation of the problem is NP-hard. This
is the second proof that we obtained in this way.

Consider the *MAX-DIFF-RATIO (MDR)* optimization problem: Given two
lists $`V=(v_{1},\dots,v_{n})`$ and $`W=(w_{1},\dots,w_{n})`$ of
positive integers, find $`j\in T\subseteq[n]`$ that maximizes

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
f(j,T)=\frac{v_{j}}{\sum_{i\in T}v_{i}}-\frac{w_{j}}{\sum_{i\in T}w_{i}}.
``` |  |

### 8.3 Machine Learning Optimization: Self-regularized Gumbel Sigmoid

Written by Lin Chen, Gang Fu, and David P. Woodruff.

#### Problem Context

Subset selection is a core problem in machine learning, relevant to
tasks like feature selection and embedding dimension optimization.
Current methods like Dropout Feature Ranking (DFR) rely on explicit
penalty terms (e.g., $`\ell_{1}`$ regularization) to control the number
of selected features. However, tuning the regularization strength
$`\lambda`$ is difficult and sensitive, often hindering practical
application. A new method, Self-regularized Gumbel Sigmoid (SrGS), was
proposed to eliminate this hyperparameter by using an implicit
regularization mechanism involving Softmax competition and budget-aware
clipping. The theoretical question was to understand exactly why and how
this parameterization enforces sparsity without an explicit penalty.

#### AI Contribution

The researchers provided the model with the mathematical definition of
SrGS and asked for a theoretical analysis of its implicit regularization
and behavior in the low-temperature limit.

- •
  Implicit $`\ell_{0}`$ Penalty: The model derived that in the
````
